chapters.title: Chapter 3: Order Flow and Price Impact

lessons.title: Trade Classification: The Lee-Ready Algorithm and Bulk Volume Classification

body.text: A raw trade print tells you a price, a quantity, and a timestamp. It does not tell you who was the aggressor, the buyer or the seller who crossed the spread to make that trade happen, and getting that one missing label right is the foundation every signed-volume and toxicity measure in this course depends on.

markDefs.definition: The side of a trade whose order crossed the spread and demanded immediate execution, as opposed to the passive resting order it matched against. A market buy hitting a resting ask makes the buyer the aggressor; a market sell hitting a resting bid makes the seller the aggressor.

children.text: Why You Need to Classify Trades at All

Order flow imbalance in the previous lesson worked directly from the book's own changes, so it never needed to know who initiated any given trade. Most trade data, though, especially historical tick data used for backtesting, arrives as a plain sequence of prints: price, quantity, and time, nothing else. To turn that into a directional signal, signed volume, a positive or negative flow you can sum over time, you first need to label each trade as buyer-initiated or seller-initiated. That labeling problem is called
, and figuring out the aggressor, the more aggressive side that crossed the spread, is the entire task.
The Tick Rule and the Quote Rule

The tick rule is the simplest classifier: if a trade prints above the previous trade's price, an uptick, classify it as buyer-initiated; below the previous price, a downtick, classify it as seller-initiated; at the same price, a zero tick, carry forward whatever the last non-zero classification was. It needs nothing but a sequence of trade prices, which makes it usable even on the sparsest historical data, at the cost of being a fairly rough approximation.

The quote rule is more direct when you have it available: compare the trade price to the prevailing bid-ask midpoint from Chapter 1 at the time of the trade. A trade above the midpoint is classified as buyer-initiated, since it means the buyer paid a price close to or at the ask, crossing the spread; a trade below the midpoint is classified as seller-initiated for the mirror reason. The one gap in the quote rule is a trade that prints exactly at the midpoint, which happens often enough in practice to need a fallback.
Lee and Ready (1991): Combining Both Rules

Lee and Ready's 1991 algorithm, still the standard reference for trade classification, uses the quote rule as its primary test and the tick rule only as a tie-breaker: if the trade price is above the midpoint, classify it as a buy; if below, classify it as a sell; if it lands exactly at the midpoint, fall back to the tick rule using the previous trade's price. This combination captures the quote rule's precision when it has a clear answer and the tick rule's ability to still produce an answer when the quote rule genuinely cannot.

body.text: Lee and Ready's original 1991 paper included a deliberate lag, comparing each trade to the quote prevailing about five seconds earlier, to account for how slowly quotes were reported relative to trades on the US markets of that era. On NSE's modern electronic order book, quotes and trades are essentially synchronized, so that specific lag does not transfer directly, but the underlying ambiguity it was designed to handle, a trade and a quote update landing close enough in time to be unclear which came first, can still occur at very short, sub-second horizons and is worth checking for in any tick-level implementation.

children.text: When Individual Trades Are Too Noisy: Bulk Volume Classification

Easley, Lopez de Prado, and O'Hara proposed a different approach in 2012, called Bulk Volume Classification, that sidesteps trade-by-trade labeling entirely. Instead of classifying each individual trade, it groups volume into buckets, either fixed time windows or fixed volume amounts, and assigns each bucket's volume a probabilistic split between buy and sell, based on how much the price moved over that bucket relative to how much it typically moves.

body.caption: Bulk Volume Classification. V is the bucket's total volume, ΔP is the price change over the bucket, σ_ΔP is the standard deviation of price changes across recent buckets, and Φ is the standard normal cumulative distribution function. Sell volume is simply V minus this buy volume.

children.text: The intuition is straightforward: a bucket where price rose sharply relative to its normal volatility was probably dominated by buy-initiated volume, so most of it gets assigned to the buy side; a bucket with little price change gets split close to evenly. Nothing here requires quote data at all, only prices and volumes, which makes bulk volume classification usable on data sources that never captured the order book, only trade prints.
Why Bulk Classification Matters for What Comes Next

Bulk volume classification is not a side note, it is the direct input to VPIN, the toxicity measure Chapter 4 builds in detail. VPIN takes exactly this buy/sell volume split, computed bucket by bucket, and tracks how imbalanced it becomes over a rolling window, using persistent imbalance as a proxy for the presence of informed trading. Everything in this lesson, both the trade-by-trade Lee-Ready approach and the bucket-based Bulk Volume Classification approach, exists to answer the same underlying question from Chapter 2's adverse selection framework: is the flow hitting this stock right now more likely to be informed or uninformed.

columns.label: Lee-Ready (Trade-by-Trade)
points: Classifies each individual trade as buyer- or seller-initiated
Needs a prevailing quote at the time of each trade, not just trade prints
Ambiguous only exactly at the midpoint, resolved by the tick rule
The original 1991 timing adjustment was built for slower, older US markets

columns.label: Bulk Volume Classification
points: Classifies volume probabilistically within a time or volume bucket, not trade by trade
Needs only price and volume; no quote data required at all
Assigns a fractional buy/sell split using the standard normal CDF of standardized price change
The direct input Chapter 4's VPIN toxicity measure is built from

body.title: Computing a Bucket's Buy Volume
body.prompt: A one-minute volume bucket trades 10,000 shares total. The price rose by ₹0.50 over the bucket, and the standard deviation of price changes across recent one-minute buckets is ₹0.50, so ΔP divided by σ equals 1.0. Using Φ(1.0) ≈ 0.8413, how many shares of the bucket's volume does Bulk Volume Classification assign to the buy side?
body.explanation: Buy volume = V × Φ(ΔP / σ) = 10,000 × 0.8413 = 8,413 shares. The remaining 1,587 shares are assigned to the sell side. A standardized price change of exactly 1.0 standard deviation is a fairly strong, though not extreme, directional move, which is why the split leans heavily toward buy volume without assigning the entire bucket to it.

body.title: Where the Tick Rule Steps In
body.question: Under the Lee-Ready algorithm, when does a trade get classified using the tick rule instead of the quote rule?
options: Every trade is classified using both rules and the results are averaged
Only when the trade price is exactly at the prevailing bid-ask midpoint
Only during the first and last fifteen minutes of the trading session
Whenever the trade volume exceeds the average daily volume for that stock
body.explanation: The quote rule is the primary classifier in Lee-Ready: any trade price above the midpoint is a buy, any trade below is a sell. The tick rule only becomes the deciding factor in the one case the quote rule cannot resolve, a trade printing exactly at the midpoint, where it falls back to comparing the trade price against the previous trade's price instead.

points: Trade classification assigns a buyer-initiated or seller-initiated label to a trade so it can be turned into signed, directional volume
The tick rule uses only the sequence of trade prices; the quote rule compares each trade to the prevailing bid-ask midpoint
The Lee-Ready algorithm uses the quote rule as its primary test and falls back to the tick rule only when a trade prints exactly at the midpoint
Lee-Ready's original quote-lag adjustment was built for slower, older markets and does not transfer directly to NSE's modern electronic book, though sub-second timing ambiguity can still occur
Bulk Volume Classification skips trade-by-trade labeling entirely, splitting each bucket's volume probabilistically using the standard normal CDF of the bucket's standardized price change
Bulk Volume Classification is the direct input to VPIN, the informed-trading toxicity measure built in Chapter 4
